posts.heading: September 13, 2026
posts.text:
The station closed its busiest day of the week with 142 feeder visits and 15 species, far exceeding the previous daily averages. This surge aligns with the installation of a new tube seed feeder in the morning and a feeder replacement in the afternoon, which resolved prior detection issues. The Tufted Titmouse dominated the visual record with 75 visits, from two minutes before sunrise to 63 minutes before sunset, while Carolina Chickadees became the most frequently heard species.

The audio source switched to a new microphone early in the day, coinciding with the first-ever detections of Carolina Chickadees, House Finches, Northern Mockingbirds, and Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. These firsts are attributable to the change in audio equipment rather than new arrivals. The visual log also marked the station’s first confident sightings of a Gray Catbird and a House Finch, the latter perched on the feeder stand.

Regulars such as the Carolina Wren, Eastern Towhee, and American Crow continued to appear, with the Wren and Towhee present on all seven recorded days of the week. In contrast, the Red-shouldered Hawk and White-breasted Nuthatch, seen earlier in the week, were absent from this day's totals. The overall activity level was significantly higher than the quiet start of the week, driven by the hardware updates.

posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged 88 feeder visits and eleven species, marking a significantly busier day than the recent average of forty-three visits. Tufted Titmice dominated the visual record with forty-nine visits, while the auditory track was led by Eastern Towhees and American Crows. This level of activity exceeds the previous week’s quieter days, such as the twenty-three visits recorded on Wednesday, though it remains comparable to the peak traffic seen on Thursday and Friday.

Mourning Dove was heard for the first time at this station. The male Northern Cardinal continued to visit the ground bowl installed earlier this week, joining a list of regulars that includes Carolina Wrens and Blue Jays. Species like the Red-shouldered Hawk and Northern Mockingbird, present earlier in the week, were absent from today’s log.

The day’s high volume aligns with the steady flow of visitors since the feeders were installed and refilled earlier this week. Tufted Titmice remained the primary feeder users, while Carolina Chickadees and Mourning Doves provided consistent secondary traffic. The station’s activity has stabilized at this higher level compared to the sparse recordings from the beginning of the week.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged 103 feeder visits and 12 species, marking a significant jump from the past week's average of 28 visits. Carolina Wrens and Tufted Titmice remained the dominant regulars, with the Wren's persistent chorus bridging the day from early morning to dusk. This level of activity contrasts with the quieter start to the week, though it follows the busy days of September 9 and 10.

A first confident visual record of an American Goldfinch was seen alongside the usual brown and gray regulars. The American Crow was the last visual record of the day, observed near the water bowl that was installed earlier in the week. Other species, including Red-shouldered Hawks and Northern Mockingbirds, were absent from today's count.

The presence of the hummingbird and the increased crow activity align with the new nectar feeder and treat bowl installed on September 7 and 10. These station changes provided new food sources utilized throughout the past few days.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The station recorded a significant increase in activity compared to the quiet start of the week, with thirteen species and ninety feeder visits far exceeding the recent daily averages. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees maintained a steady presence on the feeders, while the auditory record was dominated by the Carolina Wren and American Crow. This surge aligns with the installation of the nectar and seed feeders on September 7.

Morning highlights included the first confident visual records of Mourning Doves and White-breasted Nuthatches at this station. The Tufted Titmouse arrived before sunrise, and a Northern Mockingbird provided the final visual contact in the late afternoon.

The day ended with a dense vocal landscape, as two hundred and twenty-one detections surpassed the recent average of one hundred and seven. The station remains active with the new feeders and bowls installed over the past few days.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The day marked a sharp increase in station activity, with 22 feeder visits and 11 species recorded. The new feeders installed on September 7 explain the sudden visual activity, as the station had recorded zero visits in the preceding week. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird visited twice, once at 11:44 and again at 17:05.

Carolina Wren was the most frequently heard species, with 46 detections throughout the day. Eastern Screech-Owl calls were heard pre-dawn and again at 05:00.

Visual records included a Northern Mockingbird perched on a wire, a Tufted Titmouse visiting four times, and the first confident visual of a Carolina Chickadee.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The station closed its first active day of the week with 56 audible detections across six species, a sharp contrast to the five recorded on Monday and the silence of the days before. Red-bellied Woodpecker and Carolina Wren were the most consistent voices, appearing in multiple hourly checks from 09:00 through the 19:00 surge. American Crow, Eastern Towhee, and Blue Jay also contributed to the soundscape, while Red-shouldered Hawk made its first appearance at this location with three detections.

Despite the volume of audio, there were zero visual sightings or feeder visits all day. This lack of activity aligns with the installation of the new seed and nectar feeders at 18:00 and 20:00 yesterday evening.

This marks the station’s first recorded activity of the season. The species list includes the Red-bellied Woodpecker, American Crow, Eastern Towhee, Carolina Wren, Blue Jay, and Red-shouldered Hawk. The day’s activity was concentrated in the 09:00 and 19:00 hours, with the late evening surge driving the total count higher than any previous observation.

posts.heading: September 7, 2026
posts.text:
Two species, the Carolina Wren and Eastern Towhee, were heard for the first time here, accounting for all five detections logged.

Two new feeders were installed on the pole in the late afternoon, with one nectar and one seed unit added by six o'clock.
